name: Power posing
statement: Holding an expansive, open posture for two minutes is said to raise testosterone, lower cortisol, increase risk-taking and make a person feel more powerful.
meaning: The claim is that posture runs the causal arrow backwards. Powerful animals and powerful people spread out; the hypothesis is that spreading out makes the body and mind behave as a powerful one does. Carney, Cuddy and Yap put four outcomes on that claim at once: a hormone of dominance, a hormone of stress, a gamble, and a self-report. The four are separable, and the fate of the idea turns on keeping them apart. A person can feel more powerful after standing tall without any of it showing up in saliva or in what they do next.

origin.who: Dana R. Carney, Amy J.C. Cuddy and Andy J. Yap
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Power posing: Brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance". Its abstract ends by claiming that two one-minute poses let a person "embody power and instantly become more powerful", with "real-world, actionable implications". Gronau and colleagues, in the preprint of their 2017 meta-analysis, called the TED talk built on it the second most popular of all time.

evidence: Forty-two participants, 26 women and 16 men, were posed by an experimenter into two high-power or two low-power positions and held each for one minute. They were told the study was about electrode placement. Saliva was taken before the poses and about 17 minutes after. On testosterone the high-power group rose relative to the low-power group, F(1, 39) = 4.29, p < .05, r = .34. On cortisol it fell, F(1, 38) = 7.45, p < .02, r = .43. Offered $2 or a 50-50 die roll for $4, 86.36% of high-power posers gambled against 60% of low-power posers, chi-square(1, N = 42) = 3.86, p < .05, phi = .30. Asked how powerful and in charge they felt on a scale from 1 to 4, the high-power group averaged 2.57 against 1.83, F(1, 41) = 9.53, p < .01, r = .44. All three original authors, with Caroline Wilmuth, then ran a second experiment. Sixty-six students held a pose while preparing a mock job interview, and coders rated high-power posers higher on performance, F = 8.33, p = .005, d = 0.73, and on hireability, F = 7.22, p = .009, d = 0.68. Their own check on felt power was weaker, 2.47 against 2.04, p = .076. The accepted manuscript prints all three tests as F(1, 60), and a 2018 correction states the degrees of freedom should be 1 and 59.

replication.headline: Six preregistered studies put the feelings-of-power effect at 0.22, while the editors of the same set report virtually zero effect on any hormonal or behavioural measure.
replication.detail: Ranehill and colleagues tested 200 participants in 2015, 98 women and 102 men, holding each pose for three minutes with the experimenter blind to condition. Self-reported power replicated: a mean difference of 0.245 on the four-point scale, 95% confidence interval 0.044 to 0.446, t(193) = 2.399, p = .017, Cohen's d = 0.344. Nothing else did. Testosterone gave a mean difference of -4.077, 95% confidence interval -9.801 to 1.647, p = .162. Cortisol gave -0.028, 95% confidence interval -0.078 to 0.022, p = .272. Risk-taking in the gain domain gave -0.033, 95% confidence interval -0.085 to 0.019, p = .215. Two further behavioural tasks, risk in the loss domain and willingness to compete, also came out null. Garrison, Tang and Schmeichel preregistered a replication with 305 participants in 2016. The gamble did not move, B = -0.40, SE = 0.29, Wald = 1.92, p = .167, and felt power moved the wrong way: high-power posers reported 2.38 against 2.55, F(1, 301) = 4.87, p = .028, d = 0.26. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology then published seven preregistered studies in 2017. Preregistering the set rules out publication bias in advance, which Gronau and colleagues give as the first reason their analysis differs from earlier tallies. Six of the seven measured felt power, and Gronau and colleagues meta-analysed those 1,071 participants. Under a default prior their model-averaged estimate is 0.22, with a 95% highest density interval of 0.09 to 0.34 and a Bayes factor of 33.1 in favour of an effect. Under an informed prior it is 0.26, interval 0.14 to 0.37. Only one of the six studies was individually informative. The behavioural and hormonal side went the other way. The editors of the special issue list each of the seven studies failing its preregistered prediction, and write that there was virtually zero effect of power poses on any of the behavioural or hormonal measures. Ronay, Tybur, van Huijstee and Morssinkhof tested whether testosterone and overconfidence carry power posing through to risk-taking, and report in their abstract that they could not replicate the original findings and found no support for the extension. Gronau and colleagues state that their meta-analysis covered felt power only and did not consider behavioural or hormonal measures. Metzler and Grèzes had 82 men adopt postures repeatedly between blocks of a face-rating task in 2019. Testosterone showed no interaction of time with posture, F(2, 146) = 1.09, p = 0.340, and no main effect of posture, F(1, 73) = 0.13, p = 0.721, and cortisol and progesterone did not move either. Barel and colleagues randomised 92 young adults in 2024, with 88 in their hormone table, and found no difference between conditions on testosterone, cortisol, risk-taking or feelings of power. Within their high-power group a fall in cortisol predicted taking the gamble, b = -0.95, SE = 0.37, p = 0.011, which they call partial support for the original results on cortisol and risk-taking. Their one significant condition effect was on estradiol, among women taking oral contraceptives, F(2, 81) = 3.67, p = 0.030, and they call that finding exploratory.

study.cite: Gronau, Q. F., van Erp, S., Heck, D. W., Cesario, J., Jonas, K. J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2017). A Bayesian model-averaged meta-analysis of the power pose effect with informed and default priors: the case of felt power. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology, 2(1), 123-138.

limits: No original effect size sits in the fields above. Carney, Cuddy and Yap report theirs as correlations without intervals, r = .44 for felt power, and a correlation cannot be set against the standardised mean difference the meta-analysis gives. The replicated figure carries no interval because the one Gronau and colleagues give is a Bayesian 95% highest density interval and putting it in a frequentist field would misdescribe it. The felt-power result weakens under one obvious test. Gronau and colleagues reran the meta-analysis on the 809 participants who said they did not know the effect, and the Bayes factor fell from 33.1 to 3.1, moderate rather than very strong, with the estimate at 0.18, interval 0.03 to 0.33. Most of the six studies had not excluded people who had seen the TED talk. That is the shape a demand characteristic makes, and the authors call it something future studies should explore. Several of the papers here are served to this session as a bot challenge rather than a paywall, by Taylor and Francis and by SAGE alike. The editorial was read from the accepted manuscript deposited at Queen's University Belfast. The Gronau figures were read from the authors' PsyArXiv preprint of 1 May 2017, because the published article could not be opened. The p-curve figures below are from the typeset published article, found in an open copy, and the accepted manuscript of 6 November 2017 prints the same numbers. Ronay and colleagues' article is recorded by Unpaywall as open access at the publisher under a CC BY-NC-ND licence, and on 21 September 2026 it still could not be read: the landing page, the PDF endpoint and the epdf endpoint each returned the bot challenge, the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam repository record carries no file, and this session's egress policy blocks web.archive.org. Their conclusion here is quoted from the abstract on that repository record, which matches the abstract held by Semantic Scholar word for word. Their sample size is not stated on this page because it was not obtained. A PubMed search on 21 September 2026 for power posing and power pose returned 26 records and no multi-laboratory registered replication. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology is not indexed there, and the seven laboratories of its 2017 special issue are the nearest thing to one.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat the whole idea as dead because Dana Carney says it is. Her undated statement is candid: the sample was tiny, subjects were run in chunks with the effect checked along the way, the risk-taking p-value of .052 from a Pearson chi-square was passed over for the .05 from a likelihood ratio, and the self-report question was chosen from many that were asked. She also names a confound nobody quotes. Participants were told at once whether they had won the gamble, winning is known to raise testosterone, and high-power posers gambled more, so the hormone result may be a winning effect. All of that is evidence about how the 2010 paper was produced. Her conclusion that the effect is not real is her judgement, and a co-author's confidence is not a datum. Amy Cuddy did not follow her, and published a p-curve reply in 2018 arguing the opposite; the two should not be merged into one voice. The second error runs the other way, treating the surviving felt-power effect as vindication of the original. It is not. The 2010 paper's claim was neuroendocrine, and no study on this page recovered the testosterone or cortisol result. The two claims have opposite fates and the words 'power posing' cover both. The third error reads the two p-curves as verdicts on the same evidence. Simmons and Simonsohn started from the studies Carney, Cuddy and Yap cited in 2015, excluded nine of them, two because they measured only feelings of power, and curved the 24 p-values that remained. That set showed no evidential value: neither test for right skew passed, half p = .11 and full p = .63, the curve was flatter than one from studies with 33% average power, p = .0016, and estimated average power was 5%, with a 90% confidence interval excluding anything above 14%. Cuddy, Schultz and Fosse added 21 studies, put feelings of power back in, and curved 55. Their aggregate curve is right-skewed, half and full p both below .0001, with average power 44%. For feelings of power alone they report half p = .0009 and average power 58%. The disagreement runs wider than feelings. Their curve for emotion, affect and self-evaluation measures, which leaves feelings of power out, gives half and full p below .0001 and average power of 97%. Where the two sides agree is on the heterogeneous remainder, which gives marginal right skew at half p = .0553 and none at full p = .3601, and which Cuddy, Schultz and Fosse call very weak support for evidential value. The two papers do not even count the older literature the same way: Simmons and Simonsohn call it 33 studies, as the 2015 review does, and Cuddy, Schultz and Fosse call it 20 papers and 34 studies. The preregistered special issue is the reason the felt-power question does not rest on either. A last error is to assume the active ingredient is expanding. Elkjaer and colleagues pooled 73 studies in 2022 and found the difference sits with contractive displays against neutral ones, Hedges's g = 0.45, while expansive against neutral gave g = 0.06. Körner, Röseler and Schütz replied in the same issue, faulting that meta-analysis for not being preregistered and for missing studies. Embodied cognition, entry 54, covers the social-priming wing of the wider programme, and facial feedback is entry 3.
